analysis.one_liner: Speeds thinning of overgrown federal forests near communities by cutting environmental review, appeal windows, and court access.
analysis.headline: The bill, backed by 29 cosponsors, cleared a House committee by voice vote in October 2002 but never reached the House floor before the 107th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: After the severe 2002 wildfire season, this bill would have let the Forest Service and the Interior Department thin up to two million acres a year of fire-prone federal land near communities, water supplies, and wildlife habitat, with an abbreviated environmental analysis instead of the full review normally required. It would have shortened public comment to 21 days, compressed appeals into weeks rather than months, and sent any lawsuit to the local federal district court on a 15-day filing deadline. It also created stewardship contracts letting private companies perform the thinning and take federal timber as payment, and authorized roughly $7 billion in spending over eight years.
analysis.who_benefits: People living near overgrown federal forests, whose homes and municipal watersheds face higher wildfire risk, would get faster fuel-reduction work aimed first at the wildland-urban edge. Forestry service companies would gain paid contracts to do the thinning, and timber companies would gain access to federal timber taken as contract payment with less exposure to appeals and lawsuits.

how_it_helps.text: Reserves at least 70 percent of fuel-reduction funds for the wildland-urban interface and gives priority to projects protecting human lives and property.
Prioritizes work near municipal watersheds and water supplies and limits projects to two million acres a year, excluding wilderness areas and wilderness study areas.
Cites roughly 190 million acres of federal land at unnaturally high risk of catastrophic wildfire from fuel buildup caused by decades of fire exclusion.
Authorizes about $7 billion combined for fuel reduction on Forest Service and Interior lands across fiscal years 2004 through 2011.

analysis.who_pays: Taxpayers would fund the multi-billion-dollar program, and the public would bear reduced participation in federal land decisions: 21-day comment windows, appeals decided within weeks, a 15-day deadline to sue, and a shortened environmental analysis standing in for the full study of alternatives.
analysis.who_pays_short: Taxpayers and communities losing a say

drawbacks.text: The expedited environmental analysis would be limited to an abbreviated statement, and projects would skip the full review of alternatives required under the National Environmental Policy Act unless they build a new permanent road.

Deadlines compress public input sharply: 21 days to comment, 10 days to signal an appeal and 15 to file one, a lawsuit within 15 days in the local district court, and a court decision generally within 45 to 60 days.
The emergency title would let logging to fight bark beetles in Colorado's Routt National Forest proceed immediately with no notice, comment, appeal, or judicial review of any kind.
It would repeal the 1993 Appeals Reform Act process and require people to exhaust a new predecisional review before they could sue at all.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The underlying problem is real: decades of fire exclusion left dense fuels that threaten homes and watersheds, and concentrating money and projects on the wildland-urban edge addresses genuine risk. But the bill paid for speed with sharply reduced public participation and legal checks, including a category of logging with no judicial review at all. The same fire protection could have been pursued with fuller review; as written, the trade-off tilts toward fewer checks on federal land managers, and skeptics worried 'thinning' would open the door to broader commercial logging.

outcome.mechanism: It cleared the House Resources Committee in late October 2002, but the Agriculture Committee, which shared jurisdiction, never finished with it, and the House adjourned without ever voting.

narrative.text: Rep. Scott McInnis introduced the bill on September 4, 2002, with 18 original cosponsors, shortly after the worst fire season in decades.
The House Resources Committee ordered the bill reported as amended by voice vote on October 8 and reported it on October 31, 2002.
The House Agriculture Committee received an extension to consider the bill until November 22, 2002, but never reported it.
The bill received no House floor vote before the 107th Congress ended on January 3, 2003, and it died.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Those who wanted federal land decisions to keep full environmental review, comment, and appeal rights are better off, since nothing was enacted; communities at wildfire risk gained nothing either, and the fuel problem was left unaddressed by this bill.

for.name: Scott McInnis
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and drove it through the Resources Committee, which he served on.

for.name: James Hansen
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill and his committee held hearings, marked it up, and reported it amended by voice vote.

against.name: House Committee on Agriculture
against.what_they_did: Held the bill after the Resources Committee reported it, took an extension to November 22, and never reported it back.

against.name: Conservation organizations such as the Sierra Club and Wilderness Society
against.what_they_did: Publicly opposed the wider administration-backed effort to expedite logging and weaken environmental review on federal forests in the name of fire prevention.

sides.party_line_note: Twenty-eight of the bill's 29 cosponsors were Republicans, and it advanced through a Republican-chaired committee; one Democrat cosponsored, and the House never voted.

industries.note: Stewardship contracts would let contractors remove federal timber as payment for fuel-reduction work, with expedited review and shortened appeals lowering the cost and risk of getting that timber. The same thinning is what protects nearby communities, so the industry's gain and the public's protection are partly entangled.
The bill authorizes dozens of stewardship contracts and hundreds of millions in fuel-reduction spending, creating paid work thinning forests and restoring watersheds.
Short comment and appeal windows, a mandatory pre-review process, and tight filing deadlines would sharply narrow the ability of citizens and groups to challenge federal logging decisions in court.
